title: Shortest Paths: Dijkstra vs Repeated Relaxation
contract: Directed nonnegative integer weights, source 0. Return distances, using −1 for unreachable vertices. Weights and finite path sums fit long.
brute: long[] d=new long[n];Arrays.fill(d,INF);d[0]=0;for(int pass=1;pass<n;pass++){boolean changed=false;for(int[] edge:edges){int u=edge[0],v=edge[1];if(d[u]!=INF&&d[u]+edge[2]<d[v]){d[v]=d[u]+edge[2];changed=true;emit("Relax an edge","edge",edge,"distances",clean(d));}}if(!changed)break;}return clean(d);
optimal: List<List<int[]>> g=new ArrayList<>();for(int i=0;i<n;i++)g.add(new ArrayList<>());for(int[] edge:edges)g.get(edge[0]).add(new int[]{edge[1],edge[2]});long[] d=new long[n];Arrays.fill(d,INF);d[0]=0;PriorityQueue<long[]> q=new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingLong(x->x[1]));q.add(new long[]{0,0});while(!q.isEmpty()){long[] item=q.remove();int u=(int)item[0];if(item[1]!=d[u])continue;for(int[] edge:g.get(u))if(d[u]+edge[1]<d[edge[0]]){d[edge[0]]=d[u]+edge[1];q.add(new long[]{edge[0],d[edge[0]]});}emit("Finalize the nearest unsettled distance","vertex",u,"distances",clean(d));}return clean(d);
reasoning: Bellman–Ford repeatedly relaxes every edge and is a useful baseline, including for negative edges without reachable negative cycles.
With nonnegative weights, the smallest queued tentative distance cannot later improve through a farther vertex.
Java's PriorityQueue has no decrease-key here: insert improvements and skip stale entries. This lazy variant may hold O(E) entries; never use it with negative edges.
complexity: O(V+E log(E+1)), O(V+E) with lazy heap
